title: Philemon
summary: Philemon is a biblical book focused on grace, reconciliation, brotherhood, and costly love.
historical_context: Philemon applies the gospel to a concrete relationship involving Paul, Philemon, and Onesimus.
ancient_near_east_context: Philemon belongs to the ancient Mediterranean and Near Eastern world reflected in its setting, institutions, and canonical placement.
hebraic_worldview: Philemon should be read with attention to covenant memory, communal identity, worship, wisdom, and accountability before the Lord.
second_temple_context: Second Temple readers received Philemon as part of Israel's Scriptures and read it within questions of identity, worship, exile, and hope.
canonical_context: Within Pauline Epistles, book 13 of 13, Philemon contributes to the Bible's unfolding witness by connecting grace, reconciliation, brotherhood, and costly love to the larger storyline.
later_christian_reception: Christian interpretation has read Philemon as part of the canonical witness to faithfulness, judgment, mercy, and hope in Christ-centered Scripture reading.
literary_context: Philemon uses epistle within Pauline Epistles, book 13 of 13 to develop its themes through the book's structure and key passages.
covenantal_significance: Philemon helps readers trace covenant faithfulness, failure, mercy, and hope within its canonical setting.
authorship_positions: Traditional Pauline authorship or Pauline circle attribution
Critical scholarship debates several letters and recognizes co-workers in some correspondence
date_ranges: Some disputed letters are placed later or in the Pauline school
original_audience: Mixed Jewish-Gentile congregations and church leaders across the Roman world
historical_setting: The Greco-Roman world of mission, patronage, and local house churches
canonical_role: Philemon anchors grace, reconciliation, brotherhood, and costly love within Pauline Epistles, book 13 of 13 and connects the book to related people, places, events, and themes.
interpretive_disputes: How doctrine, ethics, and pastoral counsel fit together

related_objects.notes: Paul makes the letter's pastoral appeal.
Philemon is the recipient of the appeal.
Onesimus is the person around whom the appeal turns.
The appeal depends on grace-shaped reconciliation.
The letter calls for merciful reception of a brother.

interpretive_notes.note: Read Philemon first within its own literary setting before moving to broader canonical connections.
The relationship links on Philemon are orientation anchors, not a full interpretive outline of the book.
